newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-M&S shares down despite record profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-M&S shares down despite record profits.

text.p: Britain's biggest clothing retailer Marks and Spencer Plc said it would create 1,700 new jobs in Britain after reporting record profits for last year of more than one billion pounds ($1.6 billion).

But a slowdown in food sales, the impact of the strong pound and worries that M&S's costs were continuing to rise pushed its shares down and prompted investment analysts to cut profit forecasts for the current year.
John Richards at NatWest Markets said he was in the process of revising his forecast nearer to the 1.2 billion pound mark from 1.25 billion for 1997-98.
He said food price deflation, investment in staff and a 20 million pound hit from sterling's strength in the current year were behind the adjustment.
"Basically it's confirmation of what people have been worrying about - food deflation...costs are continuing to rise," he said.

Other retail analysts said the group's performance in food looked weaker than people had hoped for. Tony Shiret, retail analyst at Barclays de Zoete Wedd said he would bring his forecast down to 1.19 billion pounds from 1.2 billion.
M&S's shares stood 16 pence lower at 493 pence.
Food sales growth slowed to 4.5 percent in the second half of its 1996-97 year, from 6.7 percent in the first half. Food accounts for about 40 percent of M&S's total British sales.
But M&S was adamant that it would not try and boost food sales by joining the fight for customer loyalty raging between Britain's major food superstores.

M&S acknowledged the British food business was fiercely competitive and that there was currently massive price deflation partly as a result of the strong pound. But the group maintained margins last year and held market share, which it estimated at around three or four percent.
Chairman Sir Richard Greenbury said M&S's food business was slightly different from that of the mainstream stores such as Tesco Plc and J.Sainsbury Plc.
"We're not in the loyalty or discount business," he told a news conference, "It's not the way we've ever done business and I don't see why we should start."

The retailer, which now has stores in Europe, North America and Asia, will spend 1.5 billion pounds over the next three years as part of its aggressive expansion overseas as well as adding space in Britain, where it already has 286 stores.
Greenbury said M&S had increased market share in Britain in clothing and held share in food despite fierce competition.
"It's a very, very competitive environment in clothing, in foods, in retailing generally. In every single area it's competitive," he told Reuters in an interview.

Marks, the retail sector leader, is one of the clear winners in the Britain's increasingly cut-throat retail market, where food superstores and clothing shops are waging a fierce battle for sales and profits.
Last year M&S's pretax profits rose 10.9 percent to 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion), on sales up 8.7 percent to 7.84 billion. The total dividend was up 14 percent to 13 pence a share.
Greenbury said the extra British staff would not mean costs would rise faster than sales.

"People are concerned that when we take on extra staff the costs will rise faster than the sales but they haven't done that," he said. The return on sales last year was held at about 14 percent, which he said was one of the highest in the world.
The retailer will spend the bulk of the 1.5 billion pounds earmarked for expansion in Britain and continental Europe, including 30 or 40 sites in Germany, France and Spain.
The company's overseas businesses did well despite the strong pound, generating sales of 1.3 billion pounds, up nine percent and operating profits of 91 million, an increase of 23 percent.
Financial services, an increasingly important part of the group, contributed 76 million pounds to overall profit.
The group is also expanding its mail order business, and will begin a regional trial of clothing catalogues early next year. ($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
